name: Agent Negotiation in Over-the-Counter Markets
title: Agent Negotiation in Over-the-Counter Markets
answer: Agent negotiation in over-the-counter markets covers automated bilateral bargaining between software agents acting for dealers, asset managers, or corporate treasuries in instruments that trade off exchange, such as corporate bonds, interest rate swaps, foreign exchange forwards, and structured products. The scope includes price discovery, quote generation, term sheet drafting, and execution of negotiated trades where no central limit order book sets a single price. It also spans pre-trade communication, counterparty selection, and post-trade confirmation, with agents operating under limits set by their principals. The field sits within agent workflows in finance and is tracked by The AI Economist as part of its coverage of AI in market structure.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on secure messaging and API layers that connect to dealer platforms, electronic communication networks, and internal order management systems. Agents typically execute on cloud or on-premises compute with low-latency access to market data, reference data, and counterparty credit systems. They rely on natural language processing for parsing indicative quotes and term sheets, and on structured data feeds for pricing models and risk limits. Identity, authentication, and audit logging are part of the infrastructure because OTC negotiation often occurs over chat protocols and bilateral channels rather than a single exchange.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by combining large language models for dialogue and term extraction with constrained optimization or reinforcement learning for pricing and concession strategies. An agent may parse a counterparty's message, map it to a structured negotiation state, compute a counteroffer using a pricing model and inventory or risk constraints, and generate a natural language reply. Human traders set the objective, such as minimizing execution cost or maximizing spread subject to risk limits, and the agent iterates within those bounds. Some systems use multi-agent simulation to test negotiation tactics before deployment, but live agents typically operate with human approval for binding trades.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in agent negotiation turn on who is authorized to bind a firm, how negotiation records are stored, and whether the agent's behavior can be audited against the principal's instructions. Provenance requires immutable logs of every message, model version, pricing input, and approval step, because OTC trades are bilateral contracts and disputes often hinge on what was said and when. Risks include model errors that misprice a complex instrument, unauthorized disclosure of confidential positions, and manipulation or collusion if multiple agents learn to coordinate. Compliance teams review agent transcripts and model outputs under the same recordkeeping and conduct rules that apply to human traders, and liability generally remains with the deploying firm.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Agent negotiation is moving from assisted chat and quote automation toward more autonomous bargaining over standardized OTC instruments, with human oversight shifting to exception handling and limit setting. Over time, agents may negotiate across multiple counterparties simultaneously, learn from completed trades to refine concession patterns, and integrate with post-trade processing to shorten settlement cycles. The main open questions are whether regulators will accept fully automated binding negotiation for less liquid products, and how firms will manage the risk of correlated agent behavior during market stress. The AI Economist's tracking of AI-related instruments, lawsuits, and compliance pages reflects the growing attention to these systems.
